solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: asks for what the next word sounds like when spoken, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: S is the grammar abbreviation for singular
to tax is to weary or tire; TACKS is said the same way

annotation.surface: A strangely lonely note rising from an exhausted crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Weary' looks like an adjective describing the masses, but it is a verb meaning TAX, which you then hear as TACKS.
annotation.definitionFit: Stacks of something, like masses of it, means a great quantity.

entries.clue: Set fire to rubbish tips on fringes of Crowborough (5)

indicators.note: to tip something is to tip it over, turning ROT upside down
the fringes of a word are its outermost letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of Crowborough

annotation.surface: An arsonist sets light to the rubbish dumps on the edge of a Sussex town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tips' reads as rubbish dumps, which suits 'rubbish' perfectly, but it is the instruction to turn ROT over. Crowborough is a town in East Sussex.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: torch as a verb comes from the burning brand, and is the everyday word for arson.

entries.clue: Hispanic peasant is most flamboyant, endlessly in love (9)

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: CAMPEST = most flamboyant, losing its last letter T
love = nil = O, from tennis scoring

annotation.surface: A showy Latin farm worker is described as head over heels.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In love' reads as a single romantic phrase, but it splits into IN plus O.
annotation.definitionFit: Campesino is the Spanish word for a peasant farmer in Latin America.

entries.clue: Rick Stein’s head waiter ultimately suffering cramps (6)

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
the ultimate letter is the last one
to cramp is to squeeze in, so PAIN holds R

blocks.note: suffering = pain; it cramps the R

annotation.surface: The TV chef's head waiter is doubled up with cramps.
annotation.walkthrough: Rick Stein is a real TV chef, so 'Rick' passes as his first name; it is the definition, and a verb. 'Cramps' also looks like a noun but is the container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Rick is a British word for wrenching a joint slightly, a synonym for the verb.

indicators.note: to bottle is to hold inside, so BEER encloses HOLD

blocks.note: used as it stands, split BE…ER around the insert
to hold sway is to have power; hold = sway

annotation.surface: Someone keeps an eye on beer bottles as they sway about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a noun for glass containers of beer, but it is a verb meaning holds inside. 'Sway' is a noun, as in hold sway.
annotation.definitionFit: A beholder is one who looks on or watches.

entries.clue: Bravo! Hen-night do enlivened seaside city (8,3,4)

indicators.note: livened up, stirred into action, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Cheers ring out as a hen party livens up a coastal resort.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole phrase is fodder, including 'Bravo!', which looks like a mere exclamation or the NATO B. Brighton and Hove, on the English south coast, is famous for hen nights.
annotation.definitionFit: Brighton and Hove is a city on the Sussex coast, formed by joining the two towns.

annotation.surface: Offering someone only lukewarm support in a rugby selection debate.
annotation.walkthrough: The split falls where the surface doesn't suggest one: 'Partially support' reads as a single phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Halfbacks, the scrum-half and fly-half, are rugby players positioned between forwards and backs.

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it, so R enters LEAN

blocks.note: R = runs, the cricket scoring abbreviation
a plane banks, or leans, on a turn

annotation.surface: A bank manager seizes a chance, or a boss dashes into the bank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Master' and 'bank' both suggest finance or a riverbank; 'bank' is the verb to tilt, LEAN.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of acquiring a skill fully, as with a language.

indicators.note: behind means following at the back, so RODE is placed after ELECT

blocks.note: the elect = those chosen, as for salvation

annotation.surface: A bus conductor rides at the back behind a select group of passengers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' conjures a bus or an orchestra; here it is an electrical one. Blocks are listed in answer order: ELECT comes first because RODE is 'behind' it.
annotation.definitionFit: An electrode is a conductor through which electricity enters or leaves a medium.

entries.clue: First proper name to be extracted from second? (10)

indicators.note: N is pulled out of ORDINAL

blocks.clueFragment: name to be extracted from second?
blocks.note: second is an ordinal number; ORDINAL minus N (name) leaves ORDIAL

annotation.surface: A riddle about the right first name being taken from the one that comes second.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'second' is an example: it is an ordinal, like first and third. 'First' and 'second' seem a pair, but only 'First' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Primordial means existing at or from the very beginning, first in time.

blocks.note: to ape is to mimic or mock
X = kiss, as signed at the end of a letter

annotation.surface: The climax of a pretend kiss, as on stage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mock kiss' reads as a pretend kiss, with 'mock' an adjective; it is a verb meaning APE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the tip of a triangle or the high point of a career, its culmination.

annotation.surface: Someone sulks in a grumpy silence over something they want.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as a container instruction wrapping silence around something; here it simply means concerning, one piece in the sequence.
annotation.definitionFit: Shrewish means scolding and bad-tempered, like a shrew.

entries.clue: Fish louse once found in most of Bristol (6)

indicators.note: NIT sits inside the other letters
most of a thing is all but a little of it, so BOOB loses its final letter

blocks.note: Bristol = BOOB (Bristol City rhymes with titty); most of it is BOO, split BO…O
a nit is a louse egg, so a louse in its earlier state

annotation.surface: A fish louse was once found in most of the city of Bristol.
annotation.walkthrough: Bristol here is not the city: 'Bristols' is rhyming slang for breasts, from Bristol City = titty, so a Bristol is a BOOB.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: one kind of fish, a small striped tuna.

entries.clue: You initially get lecture if greengrocer’s cross (4)

indicators.note: take the initial letter of each word that follows

annotation.surface: A grumpy greengrocer threatens you with a lecture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, the greengrocer in a mood; it is a noun, a hybrid fruit.
annotation.definitionFit: The ugli is a trademarked citrus fruit, a cross between grapefruit and tangerine, sold by greengrocers.

entries.clue: Old lady, cruel at heart and dead rough (9)

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter

blocks.note: late = dead, as in the late king

annotation.surface: A granny with a cruel streak who is also very coarse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dead rough' reads as 'very rough', but it splits: 'dead' is LATE and 'rough' alone, as a verb, is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A technical sense: granulating a surface makes it grainy, roughing it up.

entries.clue: Snake wanting months to digest duck for instance (8)

indicators.note: wanting in the old sense of lacking, so the snake goes without its M
to digest is to take inside, so OCCASIN swallows O

blocks.note: MOCCASIN, a venomous snake, without M (month)
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, O

annotation.surface: A snake goes months without food and then swallows a duck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duck' suggests the bird a snake would eat, but it is cricket's zero. 'For' links: the wordplay stands for an instance.
annotation.definitionFit: An occasion is a particular instance or time something happens.

entries.clue: Unmarried state of Carol, retired mannequin (9)

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so MODEL runs backwards

annotation.surface: A former fashion model named Carol has never married.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carol' is capitalised to pass as a woman's name; it is the verb to sing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, built like kingdom or freedom from single plus the suffix for a condition.

blocks.note: a bosom friend is a close one

annotation.surface: A saucy line about a girl baring her chest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bosom' is the body part in the surface; in the wordplay it is the adjective, as in bosom pal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: revealing a secret exposes it to view.

entries.clue: Mobster, senior man, regularly used martial art (8)

indicators.note: use letters at regular intervals, every second one

blocks.note: a capo is a Mafia boss

annotation.surface: A senior gangster practises fighting skills.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Senior man' looks like a second description of the mobster, a Mafia elder; it is only a string of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Capoeira is a Brazilian martial art combining dance and acrobatics.

blocks.note: née introduces a woman's birth name
Mike is M in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: An oil tycoon was born with the name Mike.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Originally' looks like a first-letter indicator, but 'originally called' together is NÉE, the word for a maiden name.
annotation.definitionFit: The neem tree's seeds yield neem oil, used in medicine and insecticides.

indicators.note: without its top, in a down clue its first letter

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous child
of course = SURE, losing its first letter

annotation.surface: A cheeky rascal, going topless as you'd expect.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of course' is a phrase for SURE, not the word 'course'; beheading COURSE goes nowhere.
annotation.definitionFit: Impure means dirty, contaminated or morally unclean.

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the following words
read the hidden letters backwards

blocks.note: hidden across defiCIT SURplus, then read backwards

annotation.surface: A nation in the red sees its surplus turned around.
annotation.walkthrough: The economics makes 'Country' a nation; it is the adjective, as in country life.
annotation.definitionFit: Country as an adjective, as in country cottage, means rural, which is the sense here.

entries.clue: Understood one is bound by diplomacy (5)

indicators.note: something bound by a rope is enclosed by it, so I sits tied up inside TACT

annotation.surface: A diplomat realises everyone must be constrained by protocol.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Understood' reads as a verb, someone grasping a point; it is the adjective, as in an understood agreement.
annotation.definitionFit: Tacit means understood without being stated.

entries.clue: Wolf down half of most tasty sandwiches (8)

indicators.note: take half the letters of MOST
to sandwich is to hold between, so DELISH encloses MO

annotation.surface: Greedily eating up most of the tastiest sandwiches.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' is the food on the surface, but it is a verb meaning holds between. Delish is informal slang for delicious.
annotation.definitionFit: To demolish food is to eat it up quickly, to wolf it down.

indicators.note: rolling letters tumble into a new order

annotation.surface: A member of the Rolling Stones was assaulted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rolling Stone' reads as the band, but it splits into indicator and fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: dogs set on a person assault them, so the phrasal verb means attacked.

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used, a run inside the words

annotation.surface: A packet of European custard powder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Custard powder' is a real thing, so 'custard' seems part of the definition; only 'powder' is.
annotation.definitionFit: Talc is a soft mineral ground into a fine powder.

blocks.note: O = old, as in OT for Old Testament

annotation.surface: A critic declares pompous speech the defining trait of old Falstaff.
annotation.walkthrough: Falstaff is known for both bluster and bulk, so the surface suggests his windbag talk; the wordplay wants his girth.
annotation.definitionFit: Orotundity is pompous, inflated style of speech, bombast.

indicators.note: silly, crazy, so the letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: Fuming at a foolish amateur.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Daft' looks like a description of the dilettante; it is the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: An aesthete, devoted to art and beauty, can shade into a dilettante who dabbles in the arts.

entries.clue: Lining of pert setter’s winter coat (6)

indicators.note: the lining is the inside, so the inner letters

blocks.note: the setter's = mine, from the setter's point of view

annotation.surface: The lining of the crossword setter's jaunty winter coat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lining' and 'coat' make a tailoring picture, but the coat is a stoat's fur, turning white in winter.
annotation.definitionFit: Ermine is the stoat's white winter coat, prized as fur.
